Yep, Thinkpads all the way. My current daily driver is a X200 from 2008, and it works just fine. Cost me 90 Euros, including a dock. I thing the current sweet spot is the X220, still fairly cheap but powerful enough for pretty much everything. SSDs are a must.

yup I have a Lenovo Thinkpad Twist running elementaryOS

Be careful about the broadcom drivers though. I ran ArchBang on it briefly but every update broke the wifi. There are 2 drivers for the Broadcom wifi card and it would load the wrong one. So I had to disable that driver so it would load the correct one.

I had a 2013 i7 Acer Aspire that could run Arch without a hitch (apart from the expected optimus-related hiccups).

Of course, it was a POS rotbox that barely lasted more than a year before I managed to sell it off to some poor unfortunate sap a friend. Runs most linux perfectly out of the box and was very compatable with Arch but after that unfortunate experience I wouldn't use anything Acer again even if they paid me to do so...

Also, not really distro specific say, but Optimus has been (and possibly will be) a major pain in the ass on Linux. You should consider your use case and while it may be nice to have 2 graphics cards so you can choose between power and performance it really isn't as seamless a process as it is on Windows. Several times I've had optimus/bumblebee just not work for various reasons and I end up having to go into the BIOS and manually disable the GX card I don't want to use so that the system, instead of trying (and failing) to run optimus, just sees one card and works off that/

TLDR: Acer works, but will disappoint with build quality, Optimus sux

Nice :D thank you for commenting! I always wonder how much of this stuff I'm throwing out into the void is actually interesting people. Plex is a great resource for hosting your media collection in a way that lets you stream it across your LAN, Netflix style. If you don't need the over-the-internet streaming part of it (PlexPass) it's free, so there's little barrier to entry to test it out. The hardest part is loading media from DVDs. I use MakeMKV and Handbrake for that, although there's a bit of a learning curve to Handbrake.

Funny that you mention Linux support, because when I posted this I was using a Windows 8 install that I've since moved to a Fedora Linux install. There was some legwork involved in getting things running, but I love the simplicity and stability of Plex running on Linux. It's my dedicated HTPC so I don't need it to be compatible with much else aside from Plex.

It's a run rabbit hole to fall down if you enjoy tech projects, and it has a lot of practical value once you get everything up and running. I couldn't imagine my home theater setup without it.

As for installing on Linux it will depend on your Linux distribution. Plex Media Server runs on Fedora (RPM-based) and Ubuntu (DEB-based) but the frontend, Plex Home Theater, will only run on Debian based distributions like Ubuntu. That's what you'll need to go with if you want to watch movies with PHT, unless you just want to use the web UI, which is pretty nice. This is the guide I used to setup Handbrake and MakeMKV together on Fedora, which took care of the dependencies for me.

The biggest problem I had with a Linux media server was mounting my external hard drive, since it's NTFS formatted. I had to change my mount point to give my user permissions to the NTFS drive. I ended up getting some help from the guys over at /v/FixMyLinux, which is a good resource for Linux setup questions.
